item.title: Les Etats-Unis envisagent d'alléger les sanctions contre la "flotte fantôme"-responsable
item.description: L'administration américaine envisage d'alléger les sanctions contre les navires de la "flotte fantôme", qui transportent notamment du pétrole en provenance de pays comme la Russie, l'Iran ou le Venezuela, afin de faire baisser les taux de fret mondiaux, qui ont atteint des niveaux records, a dit mercredi un responsable américain.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: L'administration américaine envisage d'alléger les sanctions contre les navires de la "flotte fantôme", qui transportent notamment du pétrole en provenance de pays comme la Russie, l'Iran ou le Venezuela, afin de faire baisser les taux de fret mondiaux, qui ont atteint des niveaux records, a dit mercredi un responsable américain. Ces discussions interviennent quelques jours après que le président américain Donald Trump a temporairement levé les sanctions sur le [USN:L8N45V1O6 TEXT:"diesel russe"], une décision qui a déclenché une avalanche de critiques de la part du président ukrainien, de pays européens, et de certains élus républicains au Sénat américain. Volodimir Zelensky et les sénateurs américains ont estimé que l'accord conclu entre Washington et Moscou représentait un cadeau pour le président russe Vladimir Poutine qui permettrait à la Russie de financer sa guerre en Ukraine. Selon le responsable, les nouvelles discussions portent sur a possibilité que les Etats-Unis autorisent le transport de "pétrole légal" à bord de navires précédemment visés par des sanctions. Il s'agit donc de pétrole brut ou de produits pétroliers non visés par les sanctions de Washington, et non du pétrole russe ou iranien, qui fait l'objet de mesures punitives. L'objectif est d'augmenter les exportations de produits raffinés et de pétrole brut depuis le Golfe, a dit le responsable. Les taux de fret des pétroliers ont atteint des niveaux records, les conflits en Iran et en Ukraine ayant attisé l'inflation et rendu le pétrole brut américain inaccessible aux raffineurs asiatiques, ce qui les a poussés à se tourner vers des sources alternatives au Moyen-Orient et en Amérique latine. Le cabinet de conseil Energy Aspects a indiqué dans une note que l'assouplissement des sanctions visant la "flotte fantôme" n'aurait pas d'impact significatif sur les taux de fret, mais pourrait permettre une plus grande circulation du pétrole au Moyen-Orient. Selon des sources du secteur maritime, la levée de ces mesures ne devrait pas entraîner une baisse généralisée des taux de fret, car les assureurs maritimes resteront soumis aux réglementations de l'UE et du Royaume-Uni.

item.title: Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget
item.description: Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat.
item.dc:creator: Jan Strupczewski
item.content:encoded: Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat. Le budget de l'UE, grâce auquel le bloc finance l'ensemble de ses politiques - soutien à l'agriculture et à des industries en concurrence avec la Chine et les Etats-Unis, avancées technologiques... -, rémunère ses responsables et fournit une aide à l'Ukraine, notamment, est traditionnellement l'un des sujets les plus houleux à Bruxelles. Un consensus est nécessaire pour que le budget pluriannuel soit adopté. Celui qui est débattu, pour la période 2028-2034, est d'autant plus délicat que les finances publiques des pays membres sont soumises à des pressions accrues en raison de la hausse des prix de l'énergie et de dépenses accrues de défense. La Commission européenne a proposé l'an dernier un budget de 1.760 milliards d'euros, soit 1,26% du revenu national brut de l'UE, ce qui a provoqué un tollé parmi les contributeurs nets comme l'Allemagne, les Pays-Bas et les pays nordiques considérant que ce montant est trop élevé. Si une dernière proposition formulée en vue du sommet par l'Irlande, qui occupe la présidence tournante du bloc, fixe le budget à 1.620 milliards d'euros, les critiques ont subsisté. Le montant inclut en premier lieu 150 milliards d'euros pour le service et le remboursement du prêt commun contracté lors de la crise du COVID. Pour l'essentiel, les coupes proposées par l'Irlande concernent des dépenses de l'UE dans d'autres régions du monde et les "coussins financiers", laissant peu de marge de manoeuvre au bloc communautaire en cas d'événements imprévus. Ce projet de budget réduit aussi le financement de la recherche, de la lutte contre le changement climatique et de mesures destinées à rendre l'Europe plus compétitive. A l'inverse, sont revues à la hausse les aides apportées aux agriculteurs et les mesures destinées à améliorer les conditions de vie dans les zones rurales, alors que les politiciens européens sont désireux de conserver le soutien de cet électorat, à la taille réduite mais à la voix qui porte. D'après le centre de réflexion Bruegel, la proposition de l'Irlande préserve la structure traditionnelle - et très critiquées - du budget, centrée sur les aides aux agriculteurs et aux régions plutôt que sur le financement de mesures destinées à aider l'Europe à faire face à la concurrence de la Chine et des Etats-Unis. Seules la France et l'Allemagne peuvent permettre de sortir de l'impasse, dit Bruegel, tout en notant que les luttes politiques dans l'Hexagone en vue de l'élection présidentielle et les difficultés rencontrées par le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz, dont la cote de popularité est au plus bas, compliquent la donne. Bien que le budget doive être prêt pour 2028, les dirigeants de l'UE veulent parvenir à un accord d'ici la fin de l'année actuelle, 2027 étant marquée par des élections en France, Italie, Pologne, Grèce, Estonie, Finlande et Slovaquie, ce qui laisse entrevoir que la question du budget s'immisce dans les campagnes. Il est attendu que les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement européen organisent un sommet spécial, les 26 et 27 novembre, pour favoriser les avancées sur le budget, avec l'objectif de sceller une entente lors du sommet des 17-18 décembre.

item.title: Cost of AI default insurance spikes as data centre confidence wobbles
item.description: The cost of insuring against US tech defaults has hit record levels in the latest sign of credit stress building in the AI trade, especially for data centres dependent on future revenue.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The cost of insuring against US tech defaults has hit record levels in the latest sign of credit stress building in the AI trade, especially for data centres dependent on future revenue. The moves reflect rising investor concern over how quickly massive investments in artificial intelligence will translate into profits, and whether heavily indebted companies can generate returns fast enough to service mounting interest costs. Five-year credit default swap spreads at cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) widened by 26 basis points overnight to a record 288 bps, according S&P Global Market Intelligence. Five-year spreads for AI investor SoftBank (9984.T) widened 24 bps to 424 bps. For data-centre operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) they have blown out past 1000 bps, according to LSEG data . Credit default swap spreads show the number of basis points charged for default protection. The greater the perceived risk of a credit event, the wider the spread and Oracle's figure represents a cost of $2.88 to insure $100 worth of bonds. CoreWeave, a loss-making data-centre operator which owes nearly $50 billion according to LSEG data, is in the eye of the storm. Its debt prices are tumbling with 2032 paper changing hands at 77 cents on the dollar. Shares fell 15% on Wednesday and another 6% after market, vaporising a fifth of their value. Credit default swap spreads for Amazon (AMZN.O) , Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Meta (META.O) , and Nvidia (NVDA.O) also hit record wide levels, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though at much smaller spreads than Oracle.

item.title: TomTom to cut 200 jobs in reorganisation, targets €21 million in savings
item.description: Dutch digital mapping specialist TomTom NV said on Thursday it would cut 200 jobs globally as part of a reorganisation expected to generate annualised savings of about €21 million ($23.6 million).
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Dutch digital mapping specialist TomTom NV (TOM2.AS) said on Thursday it would cut 200 jobs globally as part of a reorganisation expected to generate annualised savings of about €21 million ($23.6 million). The company, which has been investing lately in its new mapping platform, TomTom Orbis, is gradually shifting its focus towards partnerships to develop new driving solutions, working with Microsoft (MSFT.O) on generative AI and with Mitsubishi Electric (6503.T) on automated driving, among others. "We see significant growth opportunities in automated driving and location intelligence, driven by AI," CEO Mike Schoofs said in a statement. TomTom raised its 2026 operating margin guidance to around 4% from 3% previously, including the impact of a €15 million restructuring charge in the fourth quarter. "It reflects our stronger performance year to date, as well as lower expected salary costs in Q4 resulting from the organizational realignment," the company said. TomTom also narrowed its full-year revenue expectations to between €505 and €530 million from the €495 to €555 million previously expected. It already cut [USN:L8N3SX06J TEXT:"300 jobs"] in 2025 as part of an organizational realignment to embrace AI as part of its product-led strategy. ($1 = 0.8917 euros)

item.title: Taiwan president calls for Micron, workers to negotiate 'sincerely' ahead of possible strike
item.description: Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te called on Thursday for US memory chipmaker Micron Technology and its workers to negotiate "sincerely" ahead of a possible strike by the company's union in Taiwan.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Chin Lee, Ann Wang
item.content:encoded: Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te called on Thursday for US memory chipmaker Micron Technology (MU.O) and its workers to negotiate "sincerely" ahead of a possible strike by the company's union in Taiwan. Last week, a Taiwanese union representing workers at Micron [USN:L6N45T0D9 TEXT:"said it had secured"] authorisation from its members to strike over a dispute concerning the company's bonus scheme, escalating a labour conflict at the chipmaker's largest manufacturing hub. Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan, one of its most important manufacturing hubs, and has said it invested more than T$1.6 trillion ($49.4 billion) on the island. Speaking in Taichung at the opening of a new Micron advanced assembly and testing facility, Lai said he hoped the government and private sector could work together to promote stronger communication between labour and management. "We also hope both labour and management will uphold the spirit that fish need water and water needs fish, continuing to negotiate sincerely and in good faith to build the broadest possible consensus," he added. "Only by creating harmonious labour relations can both sides win, allowing employees to work with peace of mind and businesses to move steadily and go further." Lai said he appreciated Micron's commitment to Taiwan and hoped it would continue expanding investment on the island, adding that Micron had secured government support for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) research and development. Taiwan is a crucial production hub for Micron's DRAM and HBM chips, which are used in AI servers. MICRON SEES STRONG DEMAND Manish Bhatia, Micron's president and chief operating officer, made no mention of a possible strike action in his comments delivered shortly before Lai's. "We have already sold out all the capacity for 2027 that this factory will build and we expect high-bandwidth memory to grow faster than the rest of the DRAM industry all the way through 2028," he said. Micron's Taichung union told Reuters that it looked forward to the company engaging in "more substantive dialogue and negotiations" with them. Neither Micron nor its other union, in Taoyuan, immediately responded to requests for comment on Lai's remarks. Last week, the two unions representing workers at Micron's Taoyuan and Taichung operations said they hoped the company would put forward a concrete profit-sharing proposal for employees. Mediation with the Taoyuan union ended without agreement in September, while the Taichung union remains in negotiations. The unions are encouraging members to take a day off on October 19 to join a rally in Taipei, which they said would not be a strike. ($1 = 32.3730 Taiwan dollars)

item.title: Figma CFO says design platform willing to put margins on the line to boost AI demand
item.description: Figma's CFO said on Thursday it was uncertain if the design software firm would return to peak gross margin levels as it ramps up AI spending, but said the investments will help draw users and better compete with sophisticated tools from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Sophia, Mehnaz Yasmin
item.content:encoded: Figma's CFO said on Thursday it was uncertain if the design software firm would return to peak gross margin levels as it ramps up AI spending, but said the investments will help draw users and better compete with sophisticated tools from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The company (FIG.N) has been spending heavily on AI features, including its Figma design assistant and tools that can create prototypes and web applications using text prompts, which have helped drive a steady surge in revenue, but weighed on margins. "Are we going to get back to the low-90s gross margin percentage? I don't know. But is that the thing I would be acutely focused on? No," CFO Praveer Melwani told the Reuters Global Markets Forum on the sidelines of the company's Config user conference in Bengaluru, India. Figma's quarterly gross profit margins have shrunk to the mid-80% range over the past year, down from above 90% historically. The company is betting that sacrificing margins now to boost AI adoption will help expand its user base and eventually give it room to raise prices. Figma earlier this year moved to a usage-based pricing model for AI credits on its platform. The monetization effort is expected to deliver stronger earnings in the upcoming quarters. Investors, however, have been scrutinizing finances at tech companies as they assess the returns on costly AI bets. Those concerns, coupled with worries over AI-driven disruptions, have dragged Figma's stock down about 43% this year. "I would be willing to take the hit on margin the same way that we did over the last year if it means that we're able to serve a much larger total addressable market," Melwani said. "What may be good for us may not always be what an investor is looking for... We know we're going to have the ability to take price at the right point." At Config India, Figma announced expanded access to its code layers tool, new collaborative features, and partnerships with agent platforms including OpenCode, Meta Muse and India's Sarvam AI. item.title: Ericsson braces for component cost hit after third-quarter profit beat

item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Windies' Hope worried about excess baggage after landing another Player of the Match award
item.description: West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India.
item.dc:creator: Amlan Chakraborty
item.content:encoded: West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India. The opener's unbeaten 102 in the fourth Twenty20 International on Wednesday set up a series-levelling win in Hyderabad. He also smashed a century in the second T20 in Ranchi. Hope has been in sizzling form throughout the tour, hitting two hundreds in the earlier One-Day International leg. And while he was pleased with his performances he said he was struggling to fit his awards in his luggage. "To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight," he quipped after West Indies [USN:L6N4600YY TEXT:"prevailed"] by 24 runs. "I think we are going to have some problems going back home." Hope said getting off to a good start in Hyderabad was key. "We got 50-plus opening partnership," he added. "So it was good for us to start innings and then obviously we got that foundation, you can express yourself a bit more in the middle period and then try to give the team the best finish as could as possible." Hope clobbered nine sixes in his 50-ball knock and drew the admiration of his opponents. "We need to respect what he has been doing," India opener Sanju Samson said. "He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, and respecting the bowlers as well." Hope will look to give himself more baggage problems in Saturday's series decider in Bengaluru. West Indies will next visit Bangladesh for a two-test series later this month. The hosts will breathe easier knowing Hope is being rested ahead of ODI World Cup qualifiers in February.

item.title: PetroChina to carry out its first LNG bunker fuelling in Singapore
item.description: PetroChina International on Thursday will use liquefied natural gas to bunker a vessel in Singapore for the first time, Chairman Wu Junli said, widening the alternative-fuel options it can offer shipowners at the world's top refuelling port.
item.dc:creator: Florence Tan
item.content:encoded: PetroChina International on Thursday will use liquefied natural gas to bunker a vessel in Singapore for the first time, Chairman Wu Junli said, widening the alternative-fuel options it can offer shipowners at the world's top refuelling port. The trading arm of Chinese state major PetroChina (601857.SS) was one of eight firms that received LNG bunkering licences from the Singapore government, and it also has a licence to supply methanol to ships. PetroChina will also complete the acquisition of a methanol bunker vessel on Friday, Wu told the Singapore International Bunkering conference. Citing Clarksons data, Wu said by the end of 2025, orders globally for alternative-fuel vessels had neared 2,000 ships, including more than 1,200 LNG-fuelled vessels. "Methanol-fuelled vessels are expanding rapidly, while ammonia-fuelled vessels are beginning to gain momentum," he said. However, infrastructure for emerging marine fuels significantly lags fleet development, he said, noting that the number of existing and planned methanol bunkering ports remained below 50 versus 220 LNG bunker ports worldwide. PetroChina accounted for about 10% of Singapore bunker sales last year, which exceeded 56 million metric tons. The company sold 7.95 million tons of bunker fuel globally last year and can supply 18 ports with 16 bunker vessels on time charter, he added. Last year, PetroChina completed its first commercial LNG bunkering operation in Europe and secured methanol bunkering qualification in Rotterdam in the Netherlands. China has the capacity to produce 380,000 tons per year of green methanol, Wu said.

item.title: This Chinese export boom really has legs – and wings
item.description: Overproduction at home is pushing cheap Chinese protein onto global supermarket shelves, undercutting established producers.
item.dc:creator: Daphne Zhang, Ella Cao, Lewis Jackson
item.content:encoded: In an office reeking of cigarettes, Dang Yangyang slouches on a black leather sofa in exhaustion. The general manager at Wintop Food has spent recent days chaperoning clients from Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Russia and Senegal. They all want the same thing: Chinese chicken. Wintop processes 60 million chickens annually, selling breasts, nuggets, meatballs and dumplings to more than 20 countries. Exports accounted for half of its profits last year and are underwriting 33 acres of expansion. “International clients used to distrust the quality,” Dang, 44, told Reuters during a tour of his facilities in August. “But when the meat is $1,000 cheaper per ton than Brazilian and Thai competitors, they have to either buy from China or lose out." The company is part of a wave of Chinese protein producers overcoming the country’s patchy food-safety record and leveraging additional capacity to seize space on global supermarket shelves. Changing diets at home and Beijing’s emphasis on food security have pushed companies to invest in technology and expansion. Now, they produce [USN:P8N3WQ021 TEXT:"more than China can consume"] and are unloading excess production abroad. (View the story on Reuters.com: https://www.reuters.com/world/china/this-chinese-export-boom-really-has-legs-wings-2026-10-15/) The surge in cheap Chinese protein is drawing scrutiny from Western producers and regulators, signaling fresh trade friction. The pattern echoes Beijing's strategy in steel, solar panels and electric vehicles — flooding markets with low-priced products that undercut global rivals. In July, the European Commission launched an anti-dumping probe into Pekin duck imports after local producers alleged Chinese subsidies created unfair competition. Last month, the commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 41% and 67% on Chinese pea protein. Chicken has so far avoided the same action, though European authorities are monitoring the market, a commission spokesperson told Reuters. Agriculture and food are among the few categories where China still runs a trade deficit. At just over $100 billion last year, the gap is massive but shrinking. China, already the world’s largest source of seafood exports, last year [USN:L1N44W0B4 TEXT:"became a net exporter"] of chicken. Overall, China exported $2.6 billion worth of chicken products last year, almost double 2020 levels, customs data show. Dairy exports are on track to hit $600 million this year, doubling in three years. For global consumers, the trend means cheaper protein. For foreign producers from Europe to Thailand and Brazil, it means new competitors. China’s shift from buyer to emerging exporter is having a “disruptive” effect on the global meat market, said Michael Boddington, a Beijing-based agribusiness consultant. In Asia, he said, shipments traditionally flowed in from Europe and the Americas. Now, there's a cheaper alternative — and producers globally are scrambling to compete. China’s agriculture and commerce ministries didn’t respond to Reuters questions about the country’s burgeoning protein exports. URBANITES SHUN PORK For decades, protein in China meant pork. Pigs fed the workers who built the cities and staffed the factories that powered the country's economic boom. China became home to half the world’s hogs, whose appetite for grain, especially soybeans, redrew trade flows from the US Midwest to Brazil. The country's appetite for pork provided livelihoods for small farmers like Huang Weiying, who started raising pigs in her village in Hebei province 20 years ago, owning more than 500 at a peak. But that era is over. When Reuters visited Huang in August, she was tossing slop to her last 10 hogs in a cobweb-covered barn. Some $75,000 in debt, she planned to slaughter them by autumn. “I have been raising pigs for over two decades, but it has never been as hard as the last two years,” Huang, 57, said. “Pig prices are so low. People in the cities just stopped eating pork.” The fatty pork cuts common in traditional Chinese cuisine have fallen out of favor with health-conscious urbanites. Per-capita pork consumption has fallen 13% since peaking in 2023, according to official data and state media. Chicken intake rose more than 50% per capita in the decade through 2024. Yet production kept expanding across China’s meat and dairy sectors. Officials encouraged massive buildout with subsidies targeted at large corporate producers to boost food security and rebuild herds after the 2018 [USN:KCN1RO0MO TEXT:"African swine fever outbreak"] and the covid-19 pandemic. Subsidies accounted for about 13% of Chinese agricultural producers' gross farm receipts between 2022 and 2024, according to the OECD — nearly triple the level in the early 2000s. Today, subsidized farms are contributing to overcapacity. Production has hit new highs despite an economic slowdown, tepid domestic demand and a shrinking population, government data show. Last year, China produced a record 59 million metric tons of pork; poultry output rose 7%. The dairy sector surpassed official targets for 2025 production two years early. Pork prices are hardest hit because domestic demand is weakest, but prices have also fallen for poultry and dairy. MOVING OVERSEAS For the large producers who increasingly predominate, the way out is exports. “Every Chinese livestock company is planning to expand overseas. If you want to grow, you must go abroad,” said Zhang Yuan, head of baby formula marketing at dairy giant Yili (600887.SS) , which plans to start selling formula in Southeast Asia as soon as next year. It’s a symbolic step for Asia’s largest dairy company, which had milk products pulled in a 2008 government crackdown after melamine contamination [USN:F20081006 TEXT:"sickened thousands of babies"]. The scandal turned consumers away from domestic milk for more than a decade. But Yili baby milk powder is now the top-selling brand in China. Yili’s competitor, Feihe (6186.HK) , launched its AceKid infant formula in Indonesia in April to compete with Nestlé and Mead Johnson, after bringing the product to the Philippines a year earlier. Feihe didn’t respond to requests for comment. Poultry producers are treading a similar path. At Wintop, in Shandong province, manager Dang has increased the number of chickens in each shed from 20,000 to 120,000 in a decade. The birds weigh 2.5 kg on average – compared with 2.2 kg for broilers from Brazil, according to S&P Global. They are slaughtered in under 42 days instead of 45, catching up to the 35-day US standard. The local Tengzhou government is subsidizing the wage bill for Wintop’s more than 2,000 workers, the company told Reuters without offering specifics. Tengzhou authorities didn’t respond to a request for comment. Rival processors such as Sunner are relying on higher-value processed products such as marinated chicken and ready meals to drive growth. Its overseas sales rose 42% to $135 million last year. Sunner told Reuters it is expanding the global presence of its breeds by working with countries including Uzbekistan to develop local capacity. The company developed China's first domestically bred white-feather broiler and has begun selling it in Africa and Central Asia. TOUGH COMPETITOR As Chinese producers go abroad, they are grabbing market share from established players. Chinese milk powder now competes with products from New Zealand and Europe in countries including Nigeria and Bangladesh, and is displacing Indian and Iranian producers in the Middle East, according to Yifan Li, dairy analyst at commodity broker StoneX. China has doubled its share of the European Union processed-poultry market to 10% since 2022, and tripled its share in the UK to more than 14%, according to data from Gira, a food consultancy. That growth is challenging producers such as Germany. China’s share of the Japanese market is also edging higher while the leader, Thailand, is slipping. “It’s very worrying,” said Kukrit Arepagorn, manager at the Thai Broiler Processing Exporters Association, an industry body. “Customers increasingly use cheap Chinese chicken prices as a reference point for negotiation.” Ezequiel Pires, chairman of Lisbon-based international meat trader Branexx, said his company began buying Chinese poultry in March after African customers sought cheaper alternatives to Brazilian imports. Chinese breast meat and leg quarters are 10% to 20% cheaper than Brazilian products, Pires said. China hasn’t fully shaken some of the negative associations arising from persistent food-safety scandals, analysts say. For its exporters, the challenge is to build “lasting confidence in the safety, traceability and consistency of their products," said Gordon Butland, director at Bangkok-based G&S Agriconsultants. In the EU, imported food must meet the same health and safety standards as local produce, the European Commission told Reuters. The bloc plans to strengthen EU-origin labeling, starting with poultry products in 2027. Some clients prefer Thai poultry for its consistent taste and quality, said Rupert Claxton, meat and livestock director at Gira. Still, for many customers, China’s lower price point is key. "We're exporting to whatever countries we can,” said Wintop’s Dang. “If you have a significant price advantage, many customers actively seek you out." (This story has been refiled to correct the type of duck subject to European anti-dumping probe in paragraph 6.)

item.title: Bessent calls for World Bank reforms, including upstream oil and gas financing
item.description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a long list of demands for the World Bank in line with Trump administration interests, including ending the bank's prohibition on financing upstream oil and gas projects, putting resources into deep-sea critical minerals mining and reforming its procurement policies.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent issued a long list of demands for the World Bank in line with Trump administration interests, including ending the bank's prohibition on financing upstream oil and gas projects, putting resources into deep-sea critical minerals mining and reforming its procurement policies. Bessent, in a statement issued late on Wednesday to the steering committees of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, also said that the IMF should do more to push back on countries' non-market policies that lead to global imbalances, a veiled reference to US criticism of China. Here are key highlights of the US statement: Bessent said the World Bank should take a technology-neutral approach to energy and remove constraints on natural gas and oil projects. "The Bank cannot credibly invoke country ownership while categorically excluding upstream projects before their development merits are even assessed" The US Treasury said it is making an initial contribution to a new World Bank-administered Nuclear Energy Assistance Trust Fund to help countries lay the groundwork for future nuclear power investments The Treasury said the World Bank has an important role to play in developing critical minerals mining and processing capacity. "This includes deep-sea mining, where the Bank can play a catalytic role by providing knowledge and guidance in a nascent sector," the Treasury said Bessent called for faster graduation of wealthier countries such as China and Poland from World Bank borrowing. He said the bank's project procurement policies should be reformed to not encourage subsidies, or reward distortive industrial policies, adding that it should "pursue procurement reforms that result in greater competition and quality" The Treasury said that the IMF must go further in boosting its analysis of global imbalances, including the impact of non-market policies and practices and exchange rates. "The IMF was founded to prevent these kinds of distortive policies and negative spillovers, and must exercise its voice on this critical issue or risk being sidelined"

item.title: Gulf’s latest shock imperils a rapid recovery
item.description: Visitor numbers and hotel bookings in Dubai are way off prewar levels, and Qatari GDP may shrink 16% in 2026. Lethal attacks on Saudi airports complicate an expected 2027 rebound. That could give overseas investors the jitters – right when the Gulf needs them even more.
item.dc:creator: George Hay, Afiq Fitri Alias
item.content:encoded: The Gulf’s leading economies are having a rotten year. In 2025, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates grew 1.8%, 4.6% and 6.2% respectively. In 2026, thanks to the Iran war, they'll all shrink. The latest shock, which saw Houthi missiles [USN:S8N44G01P TEXT:"hit"] Saudi’s main international [USN:L6N45Y0OR TEXT:"airport"] at the weekend, could even undermine the rapid recovery that economists expect for 2027 – and interrupt the inward flow of overseas capital that is supposed to help the region pivot away from oil. That's significant, because it's far from obvious that the countries' giant sovereign wealth funds can shoulder all the necessary investment themselves. On some metrics, the Gulf has been coping well. Following the [USN:L6N3ZO024 TEXT:"outbreak"] of war on February 28, flights operated by major regional carriers collapsed from around 2,500 a day to a few dozen, according to data from FlightRadar24. But by September, they were largely back to normal. Meanwhile, Dubai residential property prices were only off 1% year-on-year in August, according to Citi research. Yet neither of these data points give the full picture. Start with flights, which serve as a proxy for important Gulf economic activities like tourism and international business travel. Data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows that the number of airline seats scheduled on outbound flights from Dubai - a more specific yardstick of demand - fell 17% year-on-year to 4.2 million in September. This dreary picture better matches the tourism numbers. Overnight visitors to Dubai fell 44% in the first eight months of 2026 from a year earlier, per data from the emirate's tourism department. Qatari official data shows an 18% year-on-year fall in international arrivals by air in September. Saudi only saw a 13% drop in tourism numbers, but the most recent data only covers the first quarter and in any case is propped up by visitors on pilgrimage to Mecca. These figures may deteriorate further after this weekend's strikes. Hotel occupancy has also tumbled. In Dubai, it remains 15% below its year-ago level, real-estate data provider CoStar says. September's transaction volumes in Dubai residential real estate, meanwhile, are 43% below the level a year ago. Prices, which were growing at a double-digit annual percentage clip in January, are seemingly being kept afloat by cash-rich, mortgage-free owners refusing to sell. Combine all this with the oil-market mess left by a blocked Strait of Hormuz, and it's unsurprising that the International Monetary Fund is forecasting a dire 2026 for the Gulf. Saudi GDP could shrink 3.3%, the IMF reckons, compared with 3.9% for the more tourism-focused UAE. Qatar, which has no pipeline workarounds to avoid Hormuz, faces a 15.6% decline, according to the same set of forecasts. The big question is whether 2027 will be any better. The IMF thinks so: the Saudi economy will rebound by 7.9%, the fund said, assuming that Hormuz normalises in a year, with the UAE springing back 7.7%. Qatar’s economy should jump 18.8%. If US President Donald Trump uses the period after the midterm elections to strike a durable peace deal with Iran, the Gulf economic bounceback could be even stronger. Yet the risk is that a spiraling conflict, symbolised by the recent strikes on Saudi, could scupper hopes for a rosier 2027. First, the psychological shock from an attack that killed large numbers of people at one of the Gulf's main airports is unlikely to fade quickly. The most obvious risk is a major escalation by Saudi forces against the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis. This could prolong the disruption in Hormuz and the Red Sea’s [USN:L8N4520BL TEXT:"Bab el-Mandeb Strait"]. It could also mean both tourists and foreign capital stay away for longer. A prolonged conflict would also affect the region’s economic development plans, which involve shifting away from fossil fuels. These strategies are premised on giant investments by foreigners and the domestic sovereign wealth funds. A lot of the plans, like Saudi’s Vision 2030 strategy, presuppose a normalisation in how tourists and businesses view the region's security. That requires flagship events like Riyadh’s forthcoming Future Investment Initiative to be in-person, rather than forced partially online, as Reuters [USN:L6N45Z0WN TEXT:"reported"] that it may be. The sovereign-wealth behemoths, meanwhile, are not the bottomless pits of money that they sometimes appear to be. Saudi’s Public Investment Fund has over $900 billion of assets, while the UAE’s Mubadala, ADIA and L’imad collectively have around double that. The Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) has around $600 billion. But the long-running funding model for these vehicles, which involved recycling oil and gas-fuelled current account surpluses into overseas assets, has become tougher, especially at PIF. Earlier this year, in its strategy to 2030, the Saudi fund said that an undefined chunk of its financial firepower would come from raising debt and partnering with overseas investors. The Saudi need for foreign cash is especially pressing since the country no longer runs a current account surplus, meaning that its domestic investment needs exceed national savings. And PIF is far from alone in needing to court investment from Western financiers. Qatar, for example, recently launched Doha Investment , which will hold 45 state-owned companies like Qatar Airways and Qatari Diar, amounting to a third of QIA’s $580 billion of assets. It will invest abroad, but a key part of the new body's mandate is to accelerate growth at home. This, in turn, presupposes partnering with overseas investors on $60 billion worth of planned domestic developments, like national AI platform Qai and the $5.8 billion Simaisma Beach tourism project. While Doha says the move was long-planned, a 96% year-on-year fall in LNG exports and [USN:L8N44H0U3 TEXT:"$24 billion"] in lost revenues probably focused minds on the need to attract foreign money. Meanwhile, grouping together national champions like Qatar Airways may make these units more appealing for potential Western financiers eyeing debt or equity investments. If Qatar, Saudi and the UAE rebound handsomely, these sorts of projects can still work. The likes of Blackstone (BX.N) , Brookfield (BN.TO) and KKR (KKR.N) would queue up to co-invest, as they did with [USN:L6N43T0PJ TEXT:"Kuwait’s $16 billion oil pipeline"] deal in July. But Middle East airlines could collectively see $7.2 billion of net profit in 2025 become a $4.3 billion loss this year, trade body IATA has estimated . A frozen Hormuz crisis, with sporadic Houthi attacks, would subject national champions to prolonged pain. In which case the hoped-for foreign capital might not arrive – and nor would a quick Gulf rebound. Follow George Hay on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: NLCS Game 4 ticket prices plunge 50% with Dodgers in 3-0 hole
item.description: Tickets to Game 4 of the National League Championship Series have plummeted 50% with the Los Angeles Dodgers facing elimination at home against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday night.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Tickets to Game 4 of the National League Championship Series have plummeted 50% with the Los Angeles Dodgers facing elimination at home against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday night. The Dodgers let a precarious 2-1 lead in Game 3 slip away in a 6-2 loss Wednesday night and now must win consecutive games just to send the series back to Milwaukee, where the Brewers won the first two games. The get-in price for Game 4 tickets was $156 as recently as Sunday, according to TicketData.com. It had dipped to $99 before the start of Game 3 on Wednesday night, then plunged to $77 shortly after the Brewers took a commanding 3-0 series lead. Milwaukee can clinch a trip to the World Series with a win on Thursday night. A Dodgers win would force a Game 5 in Los Angeles on Friday night, with best-of-seven series potentially returning to Milwaukee for Games 6 and 7 on Sunday and Monday. Los Angeles led MLB in attendance for the 13th straight season with a total of 4.03 million to set a franchise record. There were 14 sellouts and 40 crowds of 50,000 or more at Dodger Stadium, the largest MLB ballpark (capacity 56,000). The average for 81 games was 49,805. While the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series titles in 26 years, the Brewers are on track to reach their first World Series since 1982 -- when they were in the American League. Resale tickets for a potential World Series Game 1 in Milwaukee at American Family Field (capacity 41,900) on Oct. 23 have risen 21% to $1,317 over the past three days, per TicketData. --Field Level Media

item.title: South Korea's KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech-led selloff
item.description: South Korea's benchmark stock index KOSPI fell 8% on Thursday, triggering a circuit breaker for the first time in 2-1/2 months, as chipmakers tracked a technology-led Wall Street selloff after sticky US inflation data raised bets of further rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: South Korea's benchmark stock index KOSPI fell 8% on Thursday, triggering a circuit breaker for the first time in 2-1/2 months, as chipmakers tracked a technology-led Wall Street selloff after sticky US [USN:L6N4600KR TEXT:"inflation data"] raised bets of further rate hikes. The KOSPI (.KS11) was down 480.76 points at 5,528.05, as of 0338 GMT, hitting its lowest since July 29, when trading was last halted for 20 minutes under the market's circuit-breaker mechanism. The halt marked the 10th activation of a circuit breaker on the KOSPI this year and the 16th in its history. Volatility had been stabilising since authorities tightened regulations in July to curb a retail boom in leveraged single-stock [USN:P8N44003E TEXT:"exchange-traded funds"] introduced in May. The KOSPI was headed for a seventh straight session of losses, its longest losing streak since September 2024, while index volatility (.KSVKOSPI) climbed to the highest since August 25. "The market is reacting sensitively to whether capital raising will be sustainable and whether massive infrastructure investment will lead to real income, rather than revenue growth itself in AI services," said Seo Sang-young, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities. Chipmaker Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) fell 9.70% and peer SK Hynix (000660.KS) lost 11.35%, after the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (.SOX) dropped 4.3% overnight as persistent inflation concerns fuelled expectations of further US rate hikes and hammered AI-linked stocks. The market "is struggling to find a new buyer" after buyback programmes at Samsung and SK Hynix have run their course, said Mixo Das, head of Korea equity strategy at J.P.Morgan in Hong Kong. "Over the next few weeks, we expect that process to evolve. And we think the most volatile part of this flow discovery is likely behind us. On a six- to 12-month basis, we still think that all of these AI stocks will be substantially higher than where they currently stand," Das said. Most other index heavyweights also declined, with battery maker LG Energy Solution (373220.KS) down 5.45% and Hyundai Motor (005380.KS) down 6.38%. Of the total 916 traded issues, only 52 shares advanced, while 855 declined. Foreigners were net sellers of shares worth 2.9 trillion won ($2.15 billion). The KOSPI has risen 31% so far this year, though it remains 39% below the record peak reached in late June. The won was quoted at 1,348.2 per dollar on the onshore settlement platform , 0.44% lower than its previous close at 1,342.3. The most liquid three-year Korean treasury bond yield fell by 4.4 basis points to 3.841%, while the benchmark 10-year yield fell by 5.7 basis points to 4.188%. ($1 = 1,347.5900 won)

item.title: BoE's Pill says a rate hike need not be start of long series
item.description: A future interest rate increase by the Bank of England should not be interpreted by investors as the start of a long series of increases, BoE Chief Economist Huw Pill said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: David Milliken
item.content:encoded: A future interest rate increase by the Bank of England should not be interpreted by investors as the start of a long series of increases, BoE Chief Economist Huw Pill said on Thursday. "We shouldn't give the impression that because we act now, we are on another staircase ... like we saw in 2022 and 2023. It's a different shock," Pill said during a panel discussion hosted by the Bangkok Economic Festival on the sidelines of International Monetary Fund meetings in the city. On Wednesday, Pill – who has voted for higher rates since April – had [USN:L8N4600CF TEXT:"pushed back"] against financial market bets for four rate rises over the next 12 months. Unlike the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, the BoE has kept rates on hold since the outbreak of the US-Iran war in February, but markets see a quarter-point increase after next week's meeting as a near certainty. Pill repeated his concerns that Britain was vulnerable to what he called "insidious" catch-up dynamics in inflation, as workers sought wage rises to compensate them for price rises. "You probably need to have more of a prolonged period of restriction to squeeze that," he said. Higher bond yields in advanced economies probably reflected at least in part a rise in the real neutral rate of interest needed to stabilise inflation, another factor pointing to the need for higher rates, he added.

item.title: Nordea says sharply higher interest rates may weigh on consumer confidence
item.description: Finland's Nordea Bank said on Thursday that higher interest rates could affect consumer mood in the coming months, weighing on their appetite for loans, after its quarterly operating profit missed market expectations.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Finland's Nordea Bank (NDAFI.HE) said on Thursday that higher interest rates could affect consumer mood in the coming months, weighing on their appetite for loans, after its quarterly operating profit missed market expectations. The Nordic region's biggest lender said its operating profit fell 4% to €1.54 billion ($1.73 billion) in the third quarter, while analysts had expected €1.63 billion on average, LSEG data showed. "We are mindful of the recent sharp rises in forward interest rates and the potential for higher rates to affect consumer confidence in the months to come," Nordea CEO Frank Vang-Jensen said in a statement. Third-quarter lending volumes in Nordea's personal banking unit grew 1% in constant currencies, with mortgages rising 2% mainly on strength in Sweden and Norway. Corporate lending increased 8%. As European banks kick off earnings reporting, investors will be looking for clarity on how quickly interest rate hikes could start feeding into their net interest income and profits. The European Central Bank [USN:L1N452054 TEXT:"raised interest rates"] for the second time this year in September, a move that should support Nordea in its euro zone markets, notably Finland. Norway's central bank [USN:L8N45G0I1 TEXT:"has also hiked rates"] and said it may hike again to contain inflation, while Sweden's Riksbank has so far kept rates unchanged. Sweden is Helsinki-listed Nordea's biggest individual market, where key rivals SEB (SEBa.ST) , Handelsbanken (SHBa.ST) and Swedbank (SWEDa.ST) are set to report their quarterly results later in October. Nordea's net interest income, a key metric measuring banks' income from lending and deposits, was up 1% at €1.80 billion despite lower lending margins, the bank said, broadly meeting analysts' expectations. Rising interest rates typically boost lending margins. Nordea reiterated its financial targets for 2026. ($1 = 0.8917 euros)

item.title: Morning Bid: Market picks CoreWeave as AI rout deepens
item.description: A look at the day ahead in European and global markets from Tom Westbrook
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A look at the day ahead in European and global markets from Tom Westbrook The bruising [USN:L6N460140 TEXT:"AI selloff"] extended after the bell, hard into Asia and even lent a bid to beaten-down bond markets. [USN:L6N45Z12J TEXT:"South Korea's"] chip-heavy KOSPI (.KS11) has slid more than 15% this week, though it's really data centres in the eye of the storm. Markets that last year were buyers, seeing pick-and-shovel exposure to the AI boom, are [USN:L6N45H0SG TEXT:"now worried"] they could buckle under debts before the payoff arrives from leased computer power. CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , a loss-making data-centre operator which owes nearly $50 billion according to LSEG data, was at the heart of the wipeout with shares down 15% on Wednesday and another 6% after market, vapourising a fifth of its value. Yields on its debts due in 2032 shot over 15%, sending a tremor through credit markets. In a memo, the CEO [USN:L4N4601XL TEXT:"Mike Intrator"] said markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally." The spectre of trouble in high-yield debt, especially data centres where some of their funding (and fragility) comes from chip vendors, drove investors into Treasuries and sovereign bonds around the world for the first time in a while. After spiking briefly when US CPI ran hotter than expected, ten-year US government bonds rallied and extended gains through Asia. The long bond dropped nearly 8 basis points, a big move for the timezone, and Fed funds futures surged as short-sellers raced out of the way. Beneath the shifting sentiment, the revenues flowing chipmakers' way remain enormous and growing. [USN:L1N461004 TEXT:"TSMC"] (2330.TW) , the world's largest manufacturer of AI chips, likely reports a sixth straight quarter of record earnings later on Thursday. [USN:L1N461004 TEXT:"ASML"] (ASML.AS) , the world's largest maker of tools used to make AI chips, said on Wednesday customers were already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030, easing concerns that the AI investment boom was losing momentum. Key developments that could influence markets on Thursday: - Economics: US retail sales, PPI, British monthly GDP - IMF meetings in Bangkok

item.title: Prolonged war, renewed disruptions pose biggest risk to Middle East region, IMF says
item.description: Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal
item.content:encoded: Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure. "The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability," Azour said at a news conference during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. The IMF will release a fuller outlook for the region on October 22. Pre-war surpluses, alternative routes, demand adjustments and substantial inventory drawdowns had helped contain the impact of the energy shock caused by the US-Israeli-led attacks on Iran and Tehran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz. "These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments," he said. The global lender is forecasting a deep contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region after growth of 3.3% in 2025, followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027, when growth is expected to hit 6.6%, Azour said, noting substantial differences across the region. The forecast assumes a resumption of normal trade and shipping in the first quarter of 2027, with exports gradually normalizing by mid-year and oil prices staying higher. Azour said the forecast was predicated on a quick resumption of production, noting that Qatar, for instance, had been able to accelerate its recovery despite suffering massive destruction of its natural gas capacity. But he said the shock would have a scarring impact on various sectors, with damage to infrastructure requiring additional spending, and the risks were tilted to the downside. Oil-exporting countries directly affected by the war would see a significant contraction in 2026 and a sharp rebound in growth in 2027 as energy production normalizes, but output was expected to remain below pre-war medium-term projections. The economies of oil-importing countries in the region had been resilient and were expected to remain so, he said. The Caucasus and Central Asia region had weathered the shock relatively well and inflation was expected to continue declining from elevated levels. The IMF is projecting growth to slow to 5.2% in 2026 and then 5% in 2027, from growth of 6.2% in 2025. Azour said policymakers should prioritize price stability, focus on rebuilding fiscal buffers and expand their capacity to withstand future shocks.

item.title: EU leaders to tackle China exports, energy prices, budget at summit
item.description: European Union leaders convene in Brussels on Thursday for a packed summit to debate how best to curb surging exports from China blamed by industry groups for factory closures, how to cope with high energy prices and how to bridge wide differences over the future EU budget.
item.dc:creator: Philip Blenkinsop, Kate Abnett
item.content:encoded: European Union leaders convene in Brussels on Thursday for a packed summit to debate how best to curb surging exports from China blamed by industry groups for factory closures, how to cope with high energy prices and how to bridge wide differences over the future EU budget. The leaders from the EU's 27 members meet less than a week after the European Commission secured an [USN:L6N45V0LF TEXT:"agreement with Beijing"] to limit imports of hybrid cars from China. It is a first step in what the EU hopes will be a broader plan to rein in the bloc's goods trade deficit with China that hit €360 billion ($400.4 billion) in 2025 and is on course to surpass that level this year. The next EU-China meeting is planned for March. Draft conclusions from the summit indicate leaders will request the EU executive, the Commission, to continue its dialogue with Beijing, while also making full use of EU trade defence measures and adding new trade instruments to protect the bloc further. "These imbalances are not limited to one sector. We don't have much time because every month that goes by, thousands of jobs are lost," a senior EU diplomat said. The summit comes as the bloc grapples with rising economic anxiety, which far-right parties are exploiting in elections. EU leaders tasked the Commission in June to produce concrete results in trade talks with Beijing by October. The hybrid cars deal was a first step, but the broader imbalance — spanning chemicals, steel and machinery — remains unresolved. Beijing has said that hyping up the issue of economic imbalances is an excuse to promote protectionism and exert pressure on and restrict China. GERMANY MAKES U-TURN ON CHINA IMPORTS [USN:L6N45R0Q0 TEXT:"Franco-German proposals"] released last week are likely to be the focus of discussions. The EU's two largest economies said there was an urgent need for measures to deal with imports of chemicals and PET — the plastic widely used in packaging — and called for measures to retaliate quickly against countries that harm the bloc. An [USN:L6N4600W6 TEXT:"investigation into PET"] is expected to begin soon. The paper marks a sharp turn for Germany, which only two years ago was the most vocal critic of EU anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The summit will kick off at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT) with a broad debate about EU competitiveness, of which relations with China are part. Several EU countries have also put high energy prices on the agenda, which the draft conclusions call an issue of "critical importance." The conclusions point to proposals already made by the European Commission, such as a [USN:L8N4600II TEXT:"one-year delay"] to the EU's methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports and ask the EU executive to come up with further short-term measures. EU leaders will also on Thursday discuss the [USN:L8N45Z035 TEXT:"bloc's next seven-year budget"], which requires unanimous approval and often produces the EU's most divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients. The 2028-2034 budget is no different, with a special summit set for late November to try to reach agreement. One of Friday's main topics will be the challenges facing Ukraine, with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy due to attend. Leaders are likely to discuss Ukraine's funding needs for 2027. The draft conclusions indicate leaders will also express regret over the US decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel. US President Donald Trump said at the weekend Zelenskiy [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"should be replaced"] as Ukraine's leader. Zelenskiy received a strong show of [USN:L1N4600A2 TEXT:"support in London"] on Wednesday. ($1 = 0.8991 euro)

item.title: India's IDBI Bank slides on profit booking after Fairfax buys controlling stake
item.description: IDBI Bank shares fell 6.6% on Thursday, partially unwinding the previous session's gains, after India approved the sale of a controlling stake in the lender to Fairfax in a $5.56 billion deal, the nation's biggest ever cross-border bank deal.
item.dc:creator: Kashish Tandon
item.content:encoded: IDBI Bank (IDBI.NS) shares fell 6.6% on Thursday, partially unwinding the previous session's gains, after India approved the sale of a controlling stake in the lender to Fairfax (FFH.TO) in a $5.56 billion deal, the nation's biggest ever cross-border bank deal. The stock was trading at 84.45 rupees as of 10:02 a.m. IST, set for its worst day in over a month. IDBI Bank shares surged as much as 12.9% on Wednesday ahead of the announcement of the [USN:L1N4600FH TEXT:"sale of a 61% stake"] in the lender, before ending 9% higher. "The news is materially positive for the bank and the market reaction today looks nothing more than a simple case of profit taking," said Aishvarya Dadheech, founder and CIO at Fident Asset Management. Fairfax will offer 81 rupees per share for IDBI Bank, above the benchmark price of 75.99 per share determined by the government based on fair valuations, but a 10.4% discount to the lender's closing price on Wednesday. The shift of ownership could support a gradual re-rating of IDBI Bank toward private-bank valuations, subject to improvement in growth and return ratios, according to analysts at ICICI Securities. A potential merger with CSB Bank (CSBB.NS) could add southern-market strength and a more granular franchise, they added. Fairfax currently holds a majority stake in CSB Bank. India's banking regulations do not permit one investor to have majority shareholding in multiple banks. Reuters [USN:L6N4480J0 TEXT:"reported"] in August that Fairfax would get two years to consolidate its holdings, either via a merger or a sale. BANKING SECTOR SHUFFLE Analysts say the broader trend of more foreign ownership in Indian banks is positive for the sector. IDBI Bank's acquisition fits a pattern of changing ownership in India's financial services industry, with strategic investors increasingly entering the sector, Jefferies said in a note. It comes alongside a churn in top management at large Indian lenders such as HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank. "This will keep attrition level in the industry relatively high and may keep their competitive positioning quite dynamic," analysts at Jefferies said. The sale follows investments by Emirates NBD in RBL Bank (RATB.NS) , Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp in Yes Bank (YESB.NS) and MUFG in Shriram Finance (SHMF.NS) , signalling growing overseas investment in Indian lenders after a period of steady growth and clean balance sheets. "This is yet another example that the governmental and regulatory ecosystem is increasingly intent on allowing foreign players in Indian banking," said Shivaji Thapliyal, head of research at YES Securities. Foreign equity investment in lenders could help finance loan growth across corporate, MSME and retail segments as India's funding needs expand, he added.

item.title: Late-game homers send Brewers to 3-0 NLCS advantage over Dodgers
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Jake Bauers put his team's determination on full display, getting the Milwaukee Brewers within one victory of their first World Series appearance in 44 years.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: LOS ANGELES -- Jake Bauers put his team's determination on full display, getting the Milwaukee Brewers within one victory of their first World Series appearance in 44 years. Bauers turned an 11-pitch at-bat into a go-ahead two-run homer in the seventh inning as the Brewers took a commanding 3-0 lead in the National League Championship Series with a 6-2 victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday. Milwaukee will aim for a sweep of the best-of-seven series on Thursday at Dodger Stadium. Garrett Mitchell followed Bauers with a homer of his own as the Southern California natives put on a show in front of family and friends in a ballpark where the home team has played the bully for more than a decade. "We play for each other. It's as simple as that, man," Bauers said. "Any time there's a mistake, an error, a walk, pitchers give up runs, hitters strike out in a big spot, the only thing anybody's thinking about is how can I help pick that guy up? How can I help pick that guy up and do my part to win this game?" Rookie left-hander Robert Gasser gave up three hits over five scoreless innings as the Brewers moved closer to the franchise's second trip to the World Series. The Brewers made their lone Fall Classic appearance in 1982 as an American League team, losing in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals. Jackson Chourio led off the game with a first-pitch homer off Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell as Milwaukee showed its power capabilities after finishing last in the NL in homers during the regular season with 154. "Job's not finished yet," Mitchell said. "Just got to take it a day at a time, not really worried about what's happened today, what happened yesterday or what's coming tomorrow. We've just got to show up and continue to play our brand of baseball and continue doing it for one another." Will Smith hit a two-run double for the Dodgers, who won the last two World Series titles. Los Angeles is trying to become the first NL club to win three consecutive Fall Classic championships. Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts moved Shohei Ohtani to sixth in the batting order with the superstar in a postseason slump. Ohtani went 1-for-2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch. The Dodgers' offense was held to five hits in Game 3 after collecting three in Game 2. "I haven't digested this one," Roberts said when asked about potential lineup changes for Game 4. "They're going to run a bullpen game. Just trying to figure out which guys we want to be in there, how you kind of construct the lineup, but I haven't thought about that one yet." Snell appeared to recover from Chourio's ambush home run before he was rocked by consecutive home runs with no outs in the seventh. Snell (0-1) allowed four runs on four hits over six-plus innings with two walks and nine strikeouts. "I just left the fastball over the middle to Bauers," said Snell, who was in the Tampa Bay Rays organization with Bauers from 2015-18. "... I've seen the ups and downs he's been through, and it's been a lot of downs. So for him to go through this right now, he's earned it. Hats off to him. What an at-bat." Trailing 1-0 from the jump, the Dodgers managed to put their leadoff batter on base in four of the first six innings before finally breaking through. Gasser was replaced by right-hander Abner Uribe to open the sixth, and the reliever walked three of the first four batters he faced to load the bases, including a walk to Ohtani. Smith delivered a double off the wall in left-center for a 2-1 lead after entering the game in a 1-for-25 slump. Los Angeles failed to add onto the lead in the inning against left-hander DL Hall (3-0) when Enrique Hernandez and Tommy Edman struck out to end the threat. Milwaukee responded immediately when Andrew Vaughn walked to open the seventh before Bauers' epic at-bat. Two pitches later, Mitchell went over the wall in right-center for a 4-2 advantage to end Snell's outing. Bauers had a similar plate appearance in Game 2 when he worked a 12-pitch walk with two outs in the third inning and Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single. "Yeah, there was for sure a moment where I thought to myself like, 'Oh, you're in it again,'" Bauers said. "As far as the approach for the at-bat, I didn't want to miss a fastball." The Brewers added to their lead in the eighth when Brice Turang scored on a Justin Wrobleski wild pitch, and Joey Ortiz tacked on an RBI single in the ninth. Hall threw 2 1/3 scoreless innings. Brewers closer Trevor Megill got the last four outs, striking out the final two batters, for his fourth save of the postseason. --Doug Padilla, Field Level Media

item.title: Gold rebounds from one-week low as dollar slips
item.description: Gold prices edged higher on Thursday, rebounding from a one-week low hit in the previous session, as the US dollar eased, while investors assessed the likelihood of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase this month after a hot inflation report.
item.dc:creator: Sukanya Mitra
item.content:encoded: Gold prices edged higher on Thursday, rebounding from a one-week low hit in the previous session, as the US dollar eased, while investors assessed the likelihood of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase this month after a hot inflation report. Spot gold was up 0.7% at $4,134.08 per ounce, as of 0644 GMT, after hitting its lowest since October 7 on Wednesday. US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.2% to $4,155.50. The dollar [USN:L4N46104B TEXT:"slipped"] after scaling an 18-month peak overnight. A softer dollar makes greenback-priced bullion more affordable for buyers overseas. "What we're seeing here is just the symptoms of a market uncertain about US interest rate policy, and that is resulting in a bit of volatility," said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com. "We're coming up to a really critical level for gold, which is just below the $4,000 level. If we see, again, some really strong data, then there's a view that the Fed will have to hike relatively urgently, then that will be the level of focus." [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"US consumer prices"] accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. Traders are pricing in about a 32% chance of a rate hike later this month, compared with 22% before the data, according to CME's FedWatch Tool. San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N4601CC TEXT:"Mary Daly"] said the US central bank will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further, though she signalled no need for a hike at the October 27-28 meeting. Vice Chair for Supervision [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"Michelle Bowman"] said there was time to wait and see before any more action. Although gold is viewed as an inflation hedge, higher interest rates reduce its appeal because it does not earn interest. Market focus now turns to the Producer Price Index (PPI) and retail sales data due at 1230 GMT. Among other metals, spot silver gained 0.8% to $56.08 per ounce, platinum fell 0.3% to $1,602.42 and palladium climbed 1.4% to $1,108.76.

item.title: China, North Korea open long-delayed border bridge to boost trade
item.description: China and North Korea officially opened their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions.
item.dc:creator: Florence Lo, Mandy Leong
item.content:encoded: China and North Korea officially opened their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions. Trucks festooned with the national flags of the neighbours drove across the long-delayed 3-km (2-mile) New Yalu River Bridge, its towering pylons also decked in flags, linking the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea. Knots of spectators crowded a road on the Chinese side overlooking the cable-stayed bridge completed in 2014 but unused while the North left its approach roads and customs compound unfinished. "(Bilateral) relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address at the [USN:L6N46004I TEXT:"opening"], the official Xinhua news agency said. The border crossing would "strongly promote" economic and trade cooperation and further strengthen exchanges between their people, he added. It also offers an opportunity to improve border clearance procedures, boost connectivity and build cooperation in border areas, Li said. North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also delivered a video address, Xinhua said, but the North Korea's state media have yet to report on the event. 'NO IMMEDIATE RETURN TO PRE-SANCTIONS TRADE' The opening is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past year. Despite the potential economic boost from active trade, however, analysts said North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China. "The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies. But the bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development efforts, he said. China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers with the North over the latter's missile and nuclear weapons development. China and Russia, permanent members of the UN Security Council that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans. Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang's help in fighting the war in Ukraine. DELAY WAS SETBACK FOR DANDONG'S ECONOMY The delay in opening the bridge was a [USN:L8N45U017 TEXT:"setback for Dandong"], whose economy thrived in the early 21st century as the primary trade gateway to North Korea's isolated economy. Until now, most goods have crossed about 10 km (6 miles)upstream, using an 83-year-old bridge with a rail track and a single-lane road. That remains the busiest of about 15 crossing points along the roughly 1,350-km (840-mile) border. Dandong residents welcomed the opening. "It’s been more than a decade since they first said the bridge would open... but coming here today and seeing it for myself makes me incredibly happy," said one of them, a 50-year-old surnamed He. "Once the bridge opens, this place will become much livelier, attracting more tourists," said another Dandong resident, surnamed Xie. The bridge opening was "effectively the first visible case" of adoption of agreements struck at a June summit of leaders, a South Korean Unification Ministry official said on Thursday. Seoul was monitoring whether it would lead to further practical steps as Beijing and Pyongyang seek to build their ties into a more strategic partnership, the official added. China's exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3 billion last year, an increase of 25% on the year. Still, that was well below levels before UN sanctions tightened in 2017.

item.title: UBS mulls moving headquarters from Switzerland if capital rules tighten, WSJ reports
item.description: UBS is preparing contingency plans that could include moving its headquarters out of Switzerland if lawmakers tighten the bank's capital requirements, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: UBS (UBSG.S) is preparing contingency plans that could include moving its headquarters out of Switzerland if lawmakers tighten the bank's capital requirements, the Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The options include acquiring a US financial institution and relocating, merging with a European rival, or selling itself to a US bank, the report said. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. UBS declined to comment. The European lending giant's plans come as Switzerland considers tougher "too-big-to-fail" capital rules following UBS's 2023 rescue of Credit Suisse. Under the government plan, UBS would need to hold an extra $20 billion in Common Equity Tier 1 capital, mainly by requiring its foreign units to be 100% backed by CET1 capital. Currently, they have to be at least 60% backed, largely with CET1 capital. UBS has pushed back against the proposal, saying the 100% requirement is excessive and would hurt its international competitiveness. Earlier this month, US investor Artisan Partners urged [USN:L1N45N061 TEXT:"UBS to leave Switzerland"], arguing that the planned capital requirements were "punitive" and that Switzerland was "no longer an attractive or desirable location" for the bank. Artisan estimated that proposed changes could require UBS to hold an additional $16 billion in common equity capital. However, UBS has been fending off the idea of leaving Switzerland, with Chief Executive Sergio Ermotti [USN:FWN45S1GL TEXT:"telling"] CNBC last week that staying in Switzerland was good for both the economy and shareholders. Last month, Chairman Colm Kelleher warned that UBS would need to carefully [USN:L8N4590WE TEXT:"consider its future"] in Switzerland if new banking rules became too stringent, but said the preferred outcome was to have a "Swiss [USN:L8N4590WE TEXT:"compromise "]that allows us to stay in Switzerland".

item.title: Dollar retreats from 18-month high as Treasury yields dip; Fed hike bets ease
item.description: The dollar slipped from an 18-month peak on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields amid a risk-off mood weighed on the greenback, while cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials tempered October hike expectations despite hot inflation data.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxing Li
item.content:encoded: The dollar slipped from an 18-month peak on Thursday as a sharp drop in Treasury yields amid a risk-off mood weighed on the greenback, while cautious remarks from Federal Reserve officials tempered October hike expectations despite hot inflation data. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, fell 0.2% to 101.99, giving back most of the gains it made after Wednesday's stronger-than-expected inflation figures pushed it to an 18-month high. That helped the euro bounce 0.6% from an 18-month trough to $1.1223, putting it on track for its biggest gain in nearly two months. Sterling strengthened 0.4% to $1.3250, recovering from a 13-month low. Markets turned [USN:L6N46100A TEXT:"risk-off"] as the [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"hot CPI reading"] bolstered bets on higher-for-longer Fed rates and revived worries about AI companies' heavy debt burdens, driving safe-haven flows into Treasuries. The rally in US government bonds pushed the benchmark 10-year yield to 5.0933% while the 30-year yield dipped to 5.4462%, both touching three-week lows. "The dollar has gone down in a hurry ... we think the biggest factor has been the decline in 30-year yields," said Rodrigo Catril, senior FX strategist at National Australia Bank. "If the decline in yields were to extend, the dollar could struggle, but at this stage it would suggest that the dollar is probably going to consolidate" with expectations for Fed hikes still high, he added. Market pricing for an October Fed rate hike [USN:L6N4600VL TEXT:"rose sharply"] to 50% on the back of the CPI data, before a chorus of Fed officials - including Vice Chair for Supervision [USN:L1N4600EO TEXT:"Michelle Bowman"] and San Francisco Fed President [USN:L6N4601E8 TEXT:"Mary Daly"] - said the central bank could wait for a clearer picture ahead of the October 27 and 28 meeting, tempering those bets. "Despite the whole CPI number coming slightly stronger than expected, I think markets have sort of taken the view that maybe it was not hot enough to force the Fed's hand for October," said Khoon Goh, the head of Asia research at ANZ. "(The) October (meeting) is also just a few days before the midterm elections as well," he added. "And that's possibly why the market doesn't want to be more aggressive in pricing in for October." The market's focus will now shift to US producer price (USPPM=ECI) and retail sales (USRSL=ECI) data later in the day, with the former expected to show a jump in business costs last month. Investors will also watch remarks from Fed officials including Chair Kevin Warsh at IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday for clues on the US central bank's next move. The Australian dollar fetched $0.6952 , down 0.3%, after [USN:L1N46100L TEXT:"local employment"] unexpectedly slid in September. The kiwi traded up 0.6% at $0.5626 . The Japanese yen strengthened to 157.675 per dollar and the Swiss franc was about 0.8% stronger at 0.8282. Elsewhere, the offshore yuan strengthened a touch to 6.6926 per dollar after [USN:L1N460014 TEXT:"data"] showed China's factory-gate inflation heated up last month as commodity costs rose. (This story has been corrected to fix the date for Warsh's IMF speech to Friday from Thursday, in paragraph 12.)
