item.title: Oil prices ease as investors weigh supply outlook, Middle East tensions
item.description: Oil prices fell more than 1% on Thursday as investors weighed risks to supply from attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to cut petroleum shipping costs by easing sanctions on vessels.
item.dc:creator: Sam Li, Trixie Yap
item.content:encoded: Oil prices fell more than 1% on Thursday as investors weighed risks to supply from attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to cut petroleum shipping costs by easing sanctions on vessels. Brent crude futures fell $1.76, or 1.7%, to $104.3 a barrel by 0625 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.06, or 1.1%, to $94.03, reversing gains from the previous session. WTI rose to a three-week high in the prior session after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Tehran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil prices high. A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both [USN:L1N4600JW TEXT:"sank"] near the strait in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. With the Iran war having disrupted shipping and driven up freight costs to record highs, the Trump administration is considering [USN:L1N46017R TEXT:"easing sanctions"] on so-called shadow-fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela to help ease prices, a US official said on Wednesday. The new talks centre on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. Increased output from Russia and the Middle East has kept a lid on prices. Russia's crude oil production [USN:L1N46008R TEXT:"rose"] by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd but remained down 870,000 bpd year on year, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday. The IEA also said crude oil exports from Middle East Gulf producers rose by 4.4 million bpd in September to around 75% of prewar levels. "While there is little concrete evidence of a near-term peace deal, oil continues to find its way to buyers through alternative routes and logistical arrangements," said Phillip Nova's head of market insights, Priyanka Sachdeva, in a client note. "These workarounds have helped prevent a more severe supply shock, although they come at a higher cost and leave global flows vulnerable to further disruption." In the US, crude oil and distillate inventories fell, while gasoline stocks rose last week, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks [USN:L6N4601BW TEXT:"fell by 11.1 million barrels"] in the week ended October 9, sources said. That was a much bigger draw than analysts [USN:L1N46016I TEXT:"polled"] by Reuters expected. "Despite the sharp inventory draw, oil prices barely reacted. The failure to rise on bullish news suggests investors are cautious about chasing prices higher at current levels," said Haitong Futures in a note on Thursday. Official numbers from the US Energy Information Administration are due at 12 p.m. EDT (1600 GMT), delayed by a day following the Columbus Day holiday on Monday.

item.title: Tech stocks tumble as data centre debt worries hit AI trades
item.description: Tech stocks took a beating, credit markets wobbled and bonds rallied on Thursday as crowded bets on data centres and other AI infrastructure faced a reckoning from high and rising interest rates.
item.dc:creator: Gregor Hunter
item.content:encoded: Tech stocks took a beating, credit markets wobbled and bonds rallied on Thursday as crowded bets on data centres and other AI infrastructure faced a reckoning from high and rising interest rates. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) tumbled 3.4% to tally a fourth straight day of losses, led by a plunge of more than 8% in South Korea's KOSPI (.KS11) , while the Nikkei 225 (.N225) fell 5.4%. S&P 500 e-mini futures were down 0.4%. "The selloff in Asia looks less like a sudden deterioration in technology fundamentals and more like a repricing of the cost of capital," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore. "Investors are not questioning whether AI demand exists," she said. "They are increasingly questioning what price they should pay for that growth when interest rates are high, volatile and potentially moving higher again." Overnight, [USN:L6N4601BJ TEXT:"stocks on Wall Street"] logged their third day of declines after US consumer price inflation accelerated by more than expected in September. The S&P 500 (.SPX) fell 1.1%, the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) tumbled 1.9% and a gauge of semiconductor stocks (.SOX) extended losses into a sixth day, as the prospect of [USN:L6N4601B1 TEXT:"higher interest rates"] pummelled shares of Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs. "While the initial selloff was triggered by the hotter-than-expected CPI, tech was the main driver of today’s selloff," JPMorgan analysts wrote in a note. "AI was again the main challenge ... with financing risks and IPO timelines still at the centre of the story." Asian stocks in the tech hardware supply chain were hard hit on Thursday. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (2330.TW) fell 2%, Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) plunged 9.9%, memory chipmakers SK Hynix (000660.KS) and Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) plummeted more than 11% each, and AI investor SoftBank Group (9984.T) lost more than 9%. The cost of insuring AI-linked tech giants against default has also increased, in some cases to record levels, with [USN:L4N4610DV TEXT:"credit default swaps"] widening for cloud computing giant Oracle (ORCL.N) , AI investor SoftBank (9984.T) and data-centre operator CoreWeave (CRWV.O) . Some strategists found reasons for optimism, noting that volumes were relatively light and October is typically a volatile time of year for markets. "I’m not worried, because stocks are not expensive, there is no sign of a recession, and demand still massively exceeds supply in most parts of the AI story," said Mark Matthews, head of research for Asia at Bank Julius Baer in Singapore. Defying the gloom, AI chip giant TSMC (2330.TW) posted a 69% jump in third-quarter [USN:P8N3NB03T TEXT:"net profit"] to a record T$763.1 billion ($23.59 billion) on Thursday, beating market forecasts. In early European trades, pan-region futures were down 0.9%, German DAX futures slipped 0.6% and FTSE futures were 0.2% lower. The backdrop of investor anxiety drove safe-haven buying of government bonds, with the yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond down 8.2 basis points at 5.106%. "We continue to think that yields at current levels offer decent value," DBS analysts wrote in a note. "We are not convinced that the Fed will have to deliver back-to-back hikes on the back of one set of CPI numbers." [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"The inflation data"] reshaped expectations for the Fed's rate path, with traders briefly pricing in roughly even odds of a hike later this month before scaling back those bets. Fed funds futures are now pricing an implied 75% probability the US central bank will remain on hold at the end of its next two-day meeting on October 28, little changed from a day earlier, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. "The upside surprise in US CPI and the subsequent rally in bonds is highly counterintuitive," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities. "The cleanest read through is that the slump in AI is repricing growth expectations down, leading to bonds serving as a hedge for stocks." Against the yen , the US dollar was down 0.2% at 157.975 yen, while the euro was up 0.5% at $1.1211. The Australian dollar declined 0.3% to $0.6954 after employment unexpectedly decreased by 39,300 jobs in September, against expectations of an increase of 20,000. Investor attention turns to speeches from Fed officials speaking in Bangkok, including Chair Kevin Warsh, for clues on the US central bank's next move, as well as US producer prices and retail sales data due for release later on Thursday. In [USN:L1N46101K TEXT:"oil markets"], Brent crude was down 1.3% at $104.71 a barrel as traders weighed up the effects of US sanctions relief on supply against attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: US considers easing sanctions on shadow fleet vessels to cut freight rates, official says
item.description: The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday. The discussions are happening days after President Donald Trump temporarily [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"lifted sanctions"] on Russian diesel fuel, a move met with a torrent of criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, [USN:S8N43U03J TEXT:"European"] countries and some of Trump's [USN:L1N45Z0TJ TEXT:"fellow Republicans"] in the US Senate. Both Zelenskiy and the US senators called that move a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that would provide Russia with revenue to keep funding its war in Ukraine. The new talks center on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said. That means crude or petroleum products not sanctioned by Washington rather than Russian and Iranian oil, which are under punitive measures. The goal is to get more refined products and crude out of the Gulf, the official said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a video to the World Petroleum Congress in Riyadh this week that the administration was talking about easing the sanctions on shadow fleet vessels in an effort to cut record freight rates that have cut into demand for US crude, according to Energy Aspects, a research group. Bits of the talk were broadcast on social media, but Reuters was not able to obtain the full video or a transcript. The Department of Energy said it was not available. Companies seeking to use the sanctioned vessels would have to apply to the US Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official said. The Department of Energy said any move to relieve sanctions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia to move oil or oil products. The Treasury Department referred questions to the Department of Energy. But Trump's push to move Russian diesel to global markets quickly could put pressure on the departments to allow shipment via the vessels. The White House did not respond immediately to a request for comment. High oil and fuel prices are a risk for Trump in the November 3 midterm elections in which Republicans are hoping to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. He lifted the sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7. RECORD HIGHS Tanker freight rates have [USN:L4N45U0OZ TEXT:"soared to record highs"] as the wars in Iran and Ukraine have stoked inflation and put US crude oil out of reach for Asian refiners, pushing them to seek alternatives from the Middle East and Latin America. Energy Aspects said in a note to clients that easing the sanctions on the shadow fleet would not greatly impact freight rates but could allow more movement of oil in the Middle East. Lifting the sanctions on the tankers that are mostly old and not well maintained is "unlikely to add meaningful mainstream fleet capacity overnight, especially as most tankers sanctioned over Russian or Venezuelan links have been actively trading over the past three months," it said in the note. Easing the restrictions "could make a small number of additional tankers available for certain (Strait of) Hormuz shuttle runs," in the waterway between Iran and Oman. Lifting the measures is unlikely to result in a broad easing of freight rates as ship insurers will still be bound by EU and UK regulations, maritime industry sources said.

item.title: TSMC forecasts increase in Q4 revenue after posting sixth straight quarter of record profit
item.description: TSMC, the world's largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips, said on Thursday it expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by as much as 61% from a year earlier, after posting a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings as it rides an AI boom.
item.dc:creator: Wen-Yee Lee, Ben Blanchard
item.content:encoded: TSMC, the world's largest manufacturer of advanced AI chips, said on Thursday it expects fourth-quarter revenue to rise by as much as 61% from a year earlier, after posting a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings as it rides an AI boom. The robust results should help ease concerns that the AI investment surge is losing momentum; they come a day after [USN:L6N4600AA TEXT:"ASML"] (ASML.AS) , the world's largest maker of tools used to make AI chips and advanced semiconductors, provided an upbeat outlook. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares closed down 2% ahead of the earnings release, in line with a broader tech [USN:L6N46104Y TEXT:"sell-off"] amid worries that more interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve could pummel shares of AI stocks that are sensitive to higher borrowing costs. Shares of South Korean rivals Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS) slid more than 10%. Analysts say demand for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co's (TSMC) (2330.TW) AI chipmaking capacity, as well as its advanced chip packaging technology, CoWoS, remains strong. That has catapulted Asia's most valuable company, a key supplier to Nvidia (NVDA.O) and Apple (AAPL.O) , to new heights. Its market capitalisation is almost double that of Samsung Electronics at around $2 trillion. TSMC said net profit in the July-to-September quarter hit T$763.1 billion ($23.59 billion), up 69% from a year earlier and beating a T$746.3 billion LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 16 analysts. On an earnings call following the results, TSMC said it expects fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, up from $33.73 billion a year earlier. It maintained its capital spending expectation for 2026 at $60 billion to $64 billion. The result was TSMC's highest-ever quarterly net income, as well as its 11th consecutive quarter of profit growth. Last week, it reported a 50% year-on-year rise in [USN:L6N45U0AF TEXT:"third-quarter revenue"], beating market forecasts and hitting a new record. TSMC is investing $265 billion to build chip factories in the US state of Arizona, including an additional $100 billion that was unveiled in July. In September, Reuters reported that TSMC was [USN:L6N45M06T TEXT:"evaluating"] a potential investment in Texas. Tesla CEO Elon Musk also said last week that his companies would build and operate the Terafab AI chip complex, with TSMC potentially subleasing a part of it. On its July earnings call, the company raised its capex forecast for this year to between $60 billion and $64 billion from a previous prediction at the high end of $52 billion to $56 billion. [USN:L6N4600AA TEXT:"ASML"] (ASML.AS) said on Wednesday customers were already looking to place orders for 2029 and 2030, easing concerns that the AI investment boom was losing momentum. TSMC's Taipei-listed shares have gained 57% so far this year, in line with a 62% rise for the broader Taiwanese market. ($1 = 32.3450 Taiwan dollars)

item.title: At Anthropic pre-IPO meet: ‘Thinking’ caps, surging revenue, no human extinction
item.description: Anthropic told prospective investors that revenue in the third quarter surged 45% from the prior quarter, a move that could assuage market concerns about the huge costs of developing AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Milana Vinn, Krystal Hu
item.content:encoded: Anthropic told prospective investors on Wednesday that revenue in the third quarter surged 45% from the prior quarter, two people who attended an investor day said, a move that could assuage market concerns about the huge costs of developing AI systems. Third-quarter revenue rose to $16.8 billion from $11.6 billion in the second quarter and $4.7 billion in the first quarter, the people said. Anthropic told the group the company was profitable on an adjusted basis in the third quarter, they added. The meeting in San Francisco was meant to familiarize prospective Anthropic investors with the company before its highly anticipated IPO. The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI, making Anthropic an early test of investor appetite for loss-making AI developers investing heavily to pursue massive scale. Its public-market debut is likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections , Reuters has reported. Attendees at Wednesday's event met with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and came away optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability, a few of them told Reuters as they left its headquarters in the evening. Amodei reiterated the company’s focus on AI safety but avoided mentioning threats of human extinction, one person in the group said. In its prospectus seen by Reuters last month, Anthropic warned that advanced AI could pose "catastrophic or [USN:L4N45K1J5 TEXT:"existential risks to humanity"]." On Wednesday, however, Anthropic executives talked about how the company was using its AI to help its own business including designing a custom chip. The company handed out hats to the attendees, some of which read "thinking." Anthropic could see its annual revenue run rate reach $110 billion by the end of the year, according to estimates from analysts who met with company executives earlier this week. Anthropic did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. Scrutiny of AI companies' finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centers and computing power needed to develop and operate increasingly powerful models. Targeting a valuation of over $2 trillion, Anthropic is seeking to convince investors that its breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun the enormous costs of building and running AI systems. Last year, Anthropic's revenue increased [USN:L6N45L00B TEXT:"twelvefold to"] nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters reported exclusively last month. The company has committed at least [USN:L1N45K0RM TEXT:"$518 billion over a decade"] for cloud services, computing and infrastructure. Founded by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google and Amazon (AMZN.O) , which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors. Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety, warning of the dangers posed by increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialize more powerful models. Its research has found that its own AI agents have engaged in troubling behavior in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code, though the company has said it has not seen evidence of such misalignment in real-world deployments. The Financial Times first reported the third-quarter revenue figure on Wednesday.

item.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
item.description: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk's SpaceX had restricted military-grade Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk's [USN:L8N4600M6 TEXT:"SpaceX had restricted "military-grade" Starlink services"], hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses. The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." WHAT IS STARLINK? Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX (SPCX.O) , is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers. Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions. WHAT IS STARSHIELD? Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. While its missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone. Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads. The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024. Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since [USN:L1N31S38K TEXT:"Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022"]. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque. Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the [USN:L6N41W1B2 TEXT:"Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services"] used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal. [USN:L6N4290XG TEXT:"Britain has also adopted Starshield"]. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters. Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

item.title: Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles amid surge in attacks
item.description: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Saul, Renee Maltezou
item.content:encoded: A container ship and a dry bulk carrier have both sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday. Attacks around the waterway [USN:L1N45U0E0 TEXT:"have surged over the past 10 days"], with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month. The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources. "GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday. In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organization showed on Wednesday. One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said. Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment. The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data. "MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said. "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law." GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment. "The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday. "The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage." IRAN TIGHTENS GRIP A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway. Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington. Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, [USN:L8N45Z15J TEXT:"two senior Iranian officials told Reuters."] While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk. The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.

item.title: Japan to invest up to $21 billion in two GlobalFoundries chip factories in New York
item.description: Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries , the company said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, David Shepardson, Makiko Yamazaki
item.content:encoded: Japan will invest up to $21 billion to build two chip factories in New York state that will be jointly owned by the US government and Japanese interests and operated by GlobalFoundries (GFS.O) , the company said on Wednesday. The initiative is part of a Trump administration deal struck last year for Japan to invest $550 billion in the US in return for the US lowering tariffs on Japanese cars and other imports from at least 25% to 15%. Shares of Malta, New York-based GlobalFoundries, which is majority-owned by Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund Mubadala Investment Co, rose more than 4% in afternoon trading. They have gained more than 39% this year. Construction of the first factory is scheduled to begin this year with chip production expected in 2029. GlobalFoundries executives said the partners will decide whether to build the second factory before the end of 2028. The first factory is expected to add annual US manufacturing capacity for about 900,000 300mm wafers when fully operational, ranking it among the larger US semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and create more than 1,000 factory jobs in New York. The US government previously held a 3% stake in GlobalFoundries. GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen told Reuters that will rise to 7%. Japan will provide all of the investment capital under the deal. US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the US government, which provided $1.63 billion in grants to the company, values the 7% stake in the company at more than $2 billion. "We are the first administration ever to turn grants into money for America," Trump said. Breen told Reuters initial customers for the New York factories include Japan's Renesas Electronics (6723.T) and iPhone maker Apple (AAPL.O) . On a conference call with investors, executives said the new deal will generate fees for the company for at least 20 years. This revenue is expected to be $50 million next year, when the company will earn fees for managing construction of the first factory. GlobalFoundries will shift $955 million previously awarded by the US government to accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium chip material and advanced packaging at its existing chip factories in Malta, New York, and Burlington, Vermont. GlobalFoundries' Breen said that at least some of the capital investment by Japan will flow back to chip-manufacturing toolmakers such as Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and other Japanese firms that along with US rivals dominate the supply chain. "Obviously, we have a strong interest in the Japanese equipment suppliers to be part of it," Breen said. "We will be very open-minded, but we'll definitely engage very much with the Japanese ecosystem because they have great technologies." Japan has so far announced two batches of projects worth over $100 billion combined under the overall investment scheme. Under the arrangement with the US, Trump selects projects to be funded by Japan. Available free cash flows from investments will be [USN:L1N42R099 TEXT:"split evenly"] between the two countries until a specific allocation is reached, after which 90% will go to the US. "We believe that working together with the US to expand semiconductor production capacity is highly significant for enhancing the economic security of both countries," Japanese Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa told reporters on Thursday. He rejected criticism that the investment initiative makes Japan subservient to the US, saying projects are subject to rigorous bilateral reviews to ensure they are financially viable, capable of repayment and beneficial to Japanese companies.

item.title: Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
item.description: The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office.
item.dc:creator: Richard Cowan
item.content:encoded: A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections . Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support. The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state. Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump. A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage [USN:L6N45U0XV TEXT:"to Democrats"] over his agenda. The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated [USN:L1N45R0LS TEXT:""toss-ups.""] One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held. Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races. Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat. Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base. 'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS' Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters. Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year. "I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said. Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported. "God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation. Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said. EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans. In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data. Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record. "Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union. Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear." The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law. The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices. NLRB 'DISMANTLING' When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly [USN:L2N3OO0LL TEXT:"fired"] two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted [USN:L1N3XM0FP TEXT:"for nearly a year."] Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies. "We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. [USN:L2N3S70NN TEXT:"Biden and Congress enacted programs"] to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors. Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said. OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets." A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns. Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote. Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners. "We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support. Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said. Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office. Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do." Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff."

item.title: China's Hesai launches spatial camera to boost AI-powered robotics adoption
item.description: Hesai Group , a leading Chinese autonomous driving technology firm, on Wednesday unveiled a three-dimensional mapping camera, targeting demand for physical spatial data needed to train the AI systems powering humanoid robots.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hesai Group (2525.HK) , a leading Chinese autonomous driving technology firm, on Wednesday unveiled a three-dimensional mapping camera, targeting demand for physical spatial data needed to train the AI systems powering humanoid robots. The company introduced "Kosmo," a device resembling a wine bottle, that combines lidar sensors and cameras to help developers collect real-world spatial data more efficiently. There is a significant gap in high-quality spatial data needed to train AI-powered robots to understand and interact with the real world and perform complex tasks beyond waving arms or dancing, Hesai co-founder and CEO David Li said at a launch event at the company's Shanghai factory. Li said robots remain limited in their ability to solve real productivity challenges. Most robots are still confined to low-impact functions like greeting guests, waving or dancing, he said. "What we aim to offer is essentially a platform for the underlying technologies required by the robotics industry, positioning Hesai as a tier 1 supplier comparable to Bosch in the automotive sector, or perhaps even beyond," Li said. He declined to provide revenue projections for Kosmo but said the firm has signed agreements with Chinese robotics firms to use the product. Hesai has also been developing robot actuators, which convert electricity into mechanical motion and account for more than half of a robot's material costs, Li said. Demand is growing for actuators that are lighter, smaller and more precise, allowing robots to become more safe and agile, he added. The actuators are already being used by Sharpa Robotics, a startup founded by Hesai's co-founders, in its flagship robotic hand, Sharpa Wave. A Sharpa Wave robot has been autonomously serving ice cream at a Dairy Queen outlet in Shanghai. Hesai said Kosmo's detailed mapping technology helped the robot achieve a task success rate of 99%. Sharpa Robotics, which recently raised more than 4.5 billion yuan ($672.4 million) in a funding round, operates independently of Hesai, but provides a testing ground for the company's robotics technologies. In automotive markets, Hesai has become the world's largest lidar supplier for autonomous vehicles over the past three years, driving the cost of the technology [USN:L3N3MX0MP TEXT:"below $200"] per unit. Its customers include Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) , Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) , General Motors (GM.N) and Ford Motor (F.N) . ($1 = 6.6923 Chinese yuan renminbi)

item.title: EU delays methane rules on oil and gas imports for a year
item.description: The European Commission proposed a one-year delay to the EU's methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports on Wednesday, after pressure from governments including France and the United States.
item.dc:creator: Kate Abnett
item.content:encoded: The European Commission proposed a one-year delay to the EU's methane emissions rules for oil and gas imports on Wednesday, after pressure from governments including France and the United States. The rules, due to take effect on January 1, 2027, would have required foreign oil and gas suppliers to the EU to monitor and report methane, a potent greenhouse gas. Under the proposed changes, the rules would come into force in 2028. Importers of oil and gas would have until May 31, 2029, to prove that their oil, gas and coal imports from the previous year complied with methane monitoring and reporting rules equivalent to those of the EU - meaning that their foreign suppliers would need to provide the information. "This one-year postponement of the import-related provisions is designed to help avoid additional pressures on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context," the Commission said in a statement. Methane is the second-largest contributor to climate change, after carbon dioxide. The world-first EU law was designed to tackle those emissions, which leach into the atmosphere from leaky oil and gas infrastructure around the world. But the law has faced growing political pressure after the Iran war disrupted global energy supplies and heightened concerns about fuel availability this winter. The United States, Europe's biggest liquefied natural gas supplier, warned the EU in June that the methane law could disrupt fuel deliveries, a stance backed by companies including oil major ExxonMobil (XOM.N) . The Commission moved ahead with the delay after French President Emmanuel Macron last month wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to request it, and warn the rules could create legal risks for Europe's fuel importers. Environmental groups, which say delaying the law would not address energy security concerns caused by the disruption from the Iran war, decried the delay, while industry groups called for a longer, three-year postponement. "Without a mechanism for further extensions, we risk finding ourselves in exactly the same situation 12 months from now," a spokesperson for the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers said. Those seeking a delay say that foreign oil and gas companies are not ready to comply with the EU rules and would avoid sending LNG cargoes to Europe because of the risk of fines or legal issues. EU countries and the European Parliament must negotiate and approve the delay. Some EU lawmakers and countries, including Czechia and Italy, have demanded a three-year delay and may attempt to win this in the final negotiations.

Pernod Ricard: Le CA recule moins que prévu au T1, les USA et la Chine pèsent toujours 15 octobre (Reuters) - Pernod Ricard a fait état jeudi d'une baisse moins importante que prévu de son chiffre d'affaires au troisième trimestre, le groupe de spiritueux accusant, comme anticipé, d'importants reculs en Chine et aux États-Unis. Ericsson: Le bénéfice baisse moins que prévu au T3, malgré la hausse des coûts des composants STOCKHOLM, 15 octobre (Reuters) - Le fabricant suédois d'équipements de télécommunications Ericsson a annoncé jeudi une baisse de son résultat opérationnel au troisième trimestre moins importante que prévu, tout en avertissant que la hausse des coûts des composants pèserait sur les marges l'année prochaine. France: L'inflation IPCH accélère comme prévu à +3,4% sur un an en septembre 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'inflation en France, harmonisée selon les normes européennes (IPCH), a accéléré comme attendu à +3,4% sur un an en septembre, montrent les données définitives publiées jeudi par l'Insee. La pénurie de diesel pourrait se prolonger jusqu'en 2027 selon l'AIE LONDRES, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Les tensions sur l'approvisionnement en diesel pourraient persister jusqu'en 2027 en raison d'importantes réductions de stocks, contraires à la tendance saisonnière, qui se sont combinées à une production restreinte à l'approche du pic de demande hivernal, déclare l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE) dans son rapport mensuel sur le marché pétrolier. Le Portugal choisit Lufthansa, et non Air France-KLM, pour prendre 44,9% de TAP LISBONNE, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Le gouvernement portugais a annoncé mercredi avoir choisi Lufthansa pour acquérir une participation de 44,9% dans la compagnie TAP Air Portugal, pour 1,2 milliard d'euros, Lisbonne préférant ainsi la compagnie allemande à Air France-KLM, qui avait également soumis une offre. États-Unis: Les prix à la consommation progressent en septembre, tirés par le carburant 14 octobre (Reuters) - L'inflation aux États-Unis a accéléré en septembre, en raison notamment de la hausse des prix des carburants, montrent les données officielles publiées mercredi. BlackRock: Le bénéfice bondit au 3e trimestre, la bonne tenue des marchés fait grimper les commissions 14 octobre (Reuters) - BlackRock a annoncé mercredi une forte hausse de son bénéfice au troisième trimestre, le plus grand gestionnaire d'actifs au monde ayant perçu des commissions plus élevées grâce à la gestion des fonds de ses clients. Morgan Stanley: Bénéfice en hausse au 3e trimestre, porté par les opérations sur actions 14 octobre (Reuters) - Morgan Stanley a dépassé mercredi les prévisions de bénéfice pour le troisième trimestre, citant la hausse des revenus de la banque d'investissement et la bonne tenue des opérations sur actions, dans un contexte de volatilité dû à la décision de la Réserve fédérale américaine sur les taux d’intérêt et au conflit au Moyen-Orient

item.description: Les Etats-Unis envisagent d'alléger les sanctions contre la "flotte fantôme", selon un responsable
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les Etats-Unis envisagent d'alléger les sanctions contre la "flotte fantôme", selon un responsable WASHINGTON, 14 octobre (Reuters) - L'administration américaine envisage d'alléger les sanctions contre les navires de la "flotte fantôme", qui transportent notamment du pétrole en provenance de pays comme la Russie, l'Iran ou le Venezuela, afin de faire baisser les taux de fret mondiaux, qui ont atteint des niveaux records, a dit mercredi un responsable américain. L'armée américaine envisage d'utiliser la "mère de toutes les bombes" en Iran, selon CNN 15 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée américaine a développé des plans de frappes qui pourraient inclure l'utilisation de la bombe GBU-43, la bombe conventionnelle la plus puissante jamais utilisée en zone de combats par l'armée américaine, en Iran si Donald Trump décidait de la reprise des hostilités, rapporte jeudi CNN, citant des responsables américains au fait de la question. Des frappes russes font six morts en Ukraine, les infrastructures énergétiques visées KYIV, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Des bombardements russes ont fait six morts et des dizaines de blessés mercredi à Kyiv, la capitale ukrainienne, et à Loutsk, dans l'ouest du pays, ont déclaré les autorités qui font état de dommages sur nombre d'infrastructures énergétiques. Les Houthis menacent de nouvelles attaques contre l'Arabie saoudite RYAD, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Les Houthis ont affirmé mercredi qu'ils allaient poursuivre leurs attaques contre les aéroports et les infrastructures pétrolières en Arabie saoudite dans les prochains jours, tout en revendiquant la frappe qui a endommagé mardi le siège du géant pétrolier Aramco. Sous pression, les dirigeants de l'UE envisagent d'agir face à la Chine BRUXELLES, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour examiner l'avenir de leurs relations commerciales avec la Chine, dont les exportations en forte hausse de voitures et d'autres produits manufacturés menace l'industrie locale et risquent de provoquer des licenciements massifs à travers l'Europe. Grèce: L'ambassadrice des États-Unis remerciée après des informations de presse compromettantes La Maison blanche a annoncé mardi avoir demandé à l'ambassadrice des États-Unis en Grèce de démissionner après des articles de presse indiquant elle aurait monnayé l'accès à des responsables de l'administration Trump en échange d'argent, de cadeaux et de faveurs. L'Iran utilise de nouvelles tactiques pour intensifier ses attaques avant les "midterms" aux USA selon des responsables iraniens L'Iran met en oeuvre de nouvelles tactiques pour cibler les navires transitant par le détroit d'Ormuz, dans le but de maintenir les prix du pétrole à un niveau élevé et d'influencer les élections de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis, ont déclaré deux hauts responsables iraniens à Reuters. Un ancien officier ukrainien va comparaître en Allemagne dans l'affaire Nord Stream Un ancien officier de l'armée ukrainienne, accusé d'avoir participé aux explosions survenues en 2022 sur le gazoduc Nord Stream, doit comparaître mercredi devant un tribunal allemand. Le chef de la diplomatie américaine se rendra en Inde et en Ouzbékistan ce mois-ci Le secrétaire d'Etat américain Marco Rubio se rendra en Inde et en Ouzbékistan à la fin du mois, a annoncé mardi le département d'Etat. Un navire attaqué par un drone près de la Bulgarie, 11 marins disparus Onze marins sont portés disparus mardi en mer Noire après le naufrage au large de la Bulgarie d'un navire touché par un drone.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les dirigeants de l'UE se réunissent en sommet, tensions en vue sur le budget BRUXELLES, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Les chefs d'Etat et de gouvernement de l'Union européenne se réunissent jeudi à Bruxelles pour un sommet lors duquel devraient être mises en exergue les divergences sur l'ampleur du prochain budget pluriannuel et sur les priorités de dépense du bloc communautaire, sans accord attendu dans l'immédiat. Macron va effectuer une tournée dans le Golfe, sécurité et énergie au menu PARIS, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Emmanuel Macron effectuera en début de semaine prochaine une tournée dans le Golfe afin de "poursuivre sa mobilisation" auprès de dirigeants régionaux pour revenir à la stabilité et à la libre circulation dans le détroit d'Ormuz, voie cruciale pour les livraisons énergétiques mondiales, a dit mercredi l'Elysée. Mélenchon présente un programme budgétaire censé réduire la dette de 25 milliards d'euros PARIS, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Le candidat de La France insoumise (LFI) à l'élection présidentielle, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a présenté mercredi une feuille de route budgétaire prévoyant plus de 106 milliards d'euros de recettes, 82 milliards de dépenses et une réduction de la dette publique de 25 milliards. Albanie: Manifestations étudiantes, incendie au ministère de l'Education TIRANA, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Un incendie s'est déclaré mercredi au sein du ministère albanais de l'Education, à Tirana, en marge de manifestations étudiantes émaillées de violences et de heurts avec les forces de l'ordre, qui ont fait usage de gaz lacrymogène et de canons à eau pour disperser les manifestants. Le ministre polonais des Affaires étrangères demande à Musk s'il se livre à des manœuvres politiques avec Starlink en Ukraine VARSOVIE, 14 octobre (Reuters) - Le ministre polonais des Affaires étrangères Radosław Sikorski a demandé mercredi à Elon Musk s’il "faisait de la politique" avec Starlink en Ukraine, après que Kiev eut déclaré que SpaceX avait imposé une limitation sur certains services, perturbant ainsi les missions des drones de combat. Le pape Léon XIV a passé une nuit paisible après son opération selon le Vatican CITÉ DU VATICAN, 14 octobre (Reuters) - - Le pape Léon XIV a passé une nuit paisible à l'hôpital après son intervention chirurgicale lors de laquelle le lobe inférieur de son poumon droit a été retiré, a rapporté mercredi le Vatican. Pour Lagarde (BCE), la solution aux problèmes d'endettement de la France se trouve au niveau national La France devrait résoudre ses propres difficultés sur le marché obligataire par le biais de la politique budgétaire, a déclaré mercredi la présidente de la Banque centrale européenne (BCE), Christine Lagarde, minimisant ainsi les spéculations concernant une intervention de la BCE. Le parquet antiterroriste se saisit de l'enquête sur les tirs au collège d'Aubagne Le parquet national antiterroriste a annoncé mardi se saisir de l'enquête sur l'intrusion armée au collège Joseph-Lakanal d'Aubagne (Bouches-du-Rhône) d'un élève de l'établissement qui a ouvert le feu au fusil de chasse sur le proviseur et une enseignante, les blessant légèrement. La Russie condamne la saisie par la France d'un pétrolier au large de la Réunion L'ambassade de Russie à Paris a condamné mardi la saisie par la France du navire pétrolier DF Peak à 450 milles nautiques au large de la Réunion, annoncée la veille par Emmanuel Macron, la qualifiant d'acte de piraterie et de violation du droit international. Raphaël Glucksmann remporte la primaire social-démocrate dès le premier tour Le candidat Place Publique à l'élection présidentielle, Raphaël Glucksmann, a remporté dès le premier tour la primaire social-démocrate, a annoncé dimanche le Parti socialiste.
